column2: A chariot-warrior, approaching an elephant and ranging at the head of the battle, sent it to Death with straight-jointed arrows.
Elephants, reaching horses and tossing many, put them to flight, fiercely, here and there at every moment.
Having put many horses to flight, the elephants, O king, strong and fierce, struck some with their tusks and crushed others hard.
They pierced horses with their riders in battle with their tusks, and others, mighty, seizing them, hurled them swiftly.
Struck by foot-soldiers, the elephants in the gaps on all sides gave dreadful cries of distress and fled in all ten directions.
When the foot-soldiers suddenly fled in the great battle, abandoning their ornaments, they quickly leapt about the field.
The great elephants, thinking it a sign, bent down and seized and broke the variegated ornaments.
Others, held hard on their temples and ivory-ringed tusks by lances, javelins and darts, were restrained.
Some, seizing maces from those at their side, very fierce, were cut down by chariot-warriors and horsemen and fell to the ground.
Other great elephants trampled to the ground with force a chariot and its horseman, with armour and banners.
Elephants, reaching a chariot and seizing it by the pole, O revered one, suddenly hurled it in that fierce, great battle.
A great elephant, slain by iron arrows, fell to the ground like a mountain peak shattered by the thunderbolt.
Warriors, meeting warriors in battle, struck each other with fists; seizing each other by the hair, they cut and split.
Raising an arm, one hurled another to the ground and, treading on him with a foot, struck off the quivering head.
One, O great king, struck a dead man with his feet, and another plunged a weapon into the body of one still alive.
A great fist-fight took place there among the warriors, O Bharata, and fierce hair-pulling and sheer wrestling.
One engaged with another was killed by a third unseen, who took lives in battle with weapons in many ways.
While the warriors were locked together and the confusion went on, headless trunks rose up by hundreds and thousands.
Weapons and armour drenched with blood shone like garments dyed red in a great theatre.
So that great and dreadful battle, thick with confusion, like a theatre of the mad, filled the world with its noise.
Neither their own nor the enemy were recognised, O king, by the tormented; the kings, eager for victory, fought thinking "Fight we must."
They slew their own and the enemy who came together, O great king; chaos arose among the heroes of both armies.
With broken chariots, O great king, felled elephants, fallen horses and slain men there,
the earth in an instant became impassable, a mire of flesh and blood, flowing with floods of gore.
Karna slew the Panchalas, Dhananjaya the Trigartas, and Bhimasena the Kurus and the whole elephant corps, O king.
So this destruction of the Kuru and Pandava armies took place in the afternoon, O great king, as both desired great victory.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "You tell me how the battle goes in such a way that, charioteer, I am firmly convinced there are no Kauravas left.
Duryodhana was made chariotless in that great battle; what did the son of Dharma do, and what did the king do?
How did the hair-raising fight go in the afternoon? Tell me truly, for you are skilled, Sanjaya."
[Sanjaya said:] While the armies were locked together and fighting in sections, your son, mounting another chariot, O lord of men,
seized by great anger like a venomous serpent, saw Yudhishthira, king of dharma, and said, "Charioteer, go quickly, go!
Bring me quickly there, charioteer, where the Pandava is, the king shining armoured under a held parasol."
Urged by the king, the charioteer drove the king's excellent chariot in the battle straight towards Yudhishthira.
Then Yudhishthira, enraged like an intoxicated bull, urged his charioteer: "Go to where Suyodhana is."
Casting aside his cut bow, his eyes red with rage, the son of Dharma at the head of the host took another bow.
He cut Duryodhana's banner and bow, and Duryodhana, taking another bow, pierced the Pandava in return.
Those two, greatly enraged, loosed showers of arrows at each other like two lions in fury, each wishing to conquer the other.
They struck each other, roaring like bulls, and ranged looking at each other, those two great chariot-warriors.
Then, with arrows drawn full length and loosed, each inflicting wounds on the other, those two shone, O great king, like two flowering kimshuka trees.
Then, O king, in that great fight they repeatedly made terrifying lion-roars and the sounds of palms and bows,
and the sounds of conches, those two best of charioteers, and greatly pressed each other, O great king.
Then King Yudhishthira, enraged, struck your son in the chest with three arrows, terrible, thunderbolt-swift, hard to withstand.
Your son quickly pierced the king in return with five sharp, golden-feathered arrows whetted on stone.
Then King Duryodhana, O Bharata, hurled a dart, all of iron, sharp, like a great meteor.
As it suddenly came, the king of dharma cut it with three stone-whetted arrows and pierced him with seven.
Then it fell, that great dense dart with golden shaft, falling like a great meteor and shining like fire.
Seeing his dart destroyed, your son, O lord of men, struck Yudhishthira with nine sharp broad-headed arrows.
Much pierced, that foremost of the strong, scorcher of foes, quickly took an arrow aimed at Duryodhana.
The mighty one fixed that fierce arrow on his bow, and the valiant, enraged king let it go at the king.
That arrow, reaching your son, the great chariot-warrior, stupefied the king and went into the earth.
Then Duryodhana, enraged, raising his mace, swiftly rushed at the Pandava, wishing to end the quarrel.
Seeing him with raised mace like Death with his rod, the king of dharma hurled at your son a great dart, blazing, of great speed, like a flaming great meteor.
Struck by it on his chariot in the great fight, it pierced his armour and, his heart greatly agitated, he fell and fainted.
Then Kritavarman swiftly came and took charge of your son, the king, who was sunk in an ocean of calamity.
Bhima too, taking up a great mace adorned with gold, rushed with speed at Kritavarman in the battle. Thus that fight between yours and the enemy went on.

With the sounds of elephants, chariots, men, horses and conches, delighted, and with falls of weapons of many kinds, the elephant, chariot and foot-soldier bands attacked one another facing each other.
Struck by arrows, axes, fine swords, pattishas and arrows of many kinds, elephants, chariots and horses in the great fight, and men by excellent men and by mounts—
the earth shone covered with the heads of men, with faces like lotus, sun and moon, white teeth, fine eyes and noses, and lovely crowns and earrings.
Thousands of elephants, men and horses, fleeing, struck by iron clubs, pestles, darts, javelins, claws, bhushundis and hundreds of maces, became then rivers of blood.
That army, whose men, chariots, horses and elephants were slain, dreadful to see and fierce, killed by its enemies shone, like the realm of the Fathers when creatures perish.
Then, O king, your soldiers, and your sons like sons of the gods, with the bulls of the Kurus led by the immeasurably strong, advanced in the battle against the son of Shini.
That army, crowded with the best men, horses, chariots and elephants, very beautiful and terrible, roaring like the salt ocean, resembled the army of gods and asuras.
Then, equal in valour to the lord of the gods, the son of Avi struck the hero of the Shinis in the battle with arrows bright as the sun's rays, like a younger brother of the best of the gods.
Then the mighty one, friend of Drupada's son, swiftly attacked him who was like the ocean and pressed by the swifter foe, and wrought great havoc of men, chariots, horses and elephants.
Then the two best of men, having performed their daily rites and duly worshipped the Lord Bhava, quickly came to your army, resolved to slay their foes—Arjuna and Keshava.
The foes saw, their minds captured, the chariot approaching nearby, with the sound of thunder-clouds, its banner fluttering in the wind, drawn by white horses.
Then, stretching Gandiva, Arjuna as if dancing in the battle filled the sky, the quarters and intermediate quarters with arrows.
He smote chariots like aerial cars, with their machines, weapons and banners, and with their charioteers, with arrows, as the wind scatters clouds.
With arrows he sent to Yama's abode elephants and their drivers, with banners and weapons, horsemen, horses and foot-soldiers.
Duryodhana alone advanced against that great chariot-warrior, irresistible, enraged like Death, striking at him with arrows of various kinds.
Arjuna killed his bow, charioteer, standard and horses with seven arrows, and cut the parasol with a feathered arrow.
When he reached the ninth, he loosed a counter-striking arrow; Drona's son cut that excellent arrow aimed at Duryodhana into seven.
Then cutting Drona's son's bow and killing his best horses with arrows, the Pandava cut the very formidable bow of Kripa too.
Cutting Hardikya's bow, he killed his banner and horses; and cutting Duhshasana's excellent arrow, he went on to Radheya.
Then Karna, leaving Satyaki, swiftly pierced Arjuna with three and Krishna with twenty, and Partha again with three.
Then Satyaki came and, piercing Karna with sharp arrows, tormented him again with ninety-nine and fierce ones, and with a hundred.
Then all the heroes of the Pandavas pressed Karna—Yudhamanyu, Shikhandin, the sons of Draupadi, the Prabhadrakas,
Uttamaujas, Yuyutsu, the twins and the Parshata, the force of the Chedis, Karushas, Matsyas and Kekayas, the strong Chekitana and the king of dharma of good vows.

These, with chariots, horses, elephants and foot-soldiers of fierce valour, surrounding Karna in the battle, showered him with weapons of many kinds, speaking fierce words, all bent on Karna's slaying.
Cutting that shower of weapons in many ways with sharp arrows, Karna drove them all away, like the wind breaking trees.
Karna was seen enraged slaying chariot-warriors with their chief officers, elephants, horses with riders and flocks of foot-soldiers.
The Pandava army, slain by the splendour of Karna's weapons, weaponless and wounded in body, mostly turned away.
Then Arjuna himself, countering Karna's weapon with a weapon, covered the quarters, sky and earth with showers of arrows.
Arrows fell like pestles, like iron clubs, others like shataghnis, others like fierce thunderbolts.
Slain by them, that army with its foot-soldiers, horses, chariots and elephants wandered everywhere with eyes shut tight.
Then it became a battle entirely of horses, men and elephants; others, slain by arrows, fled in fear.
Thus, while they were engaged in battle, eager for victory, the sun reached the mountain of setting.
From darkness, O great king, and especially from dust, we could see nothing, auspicious or inauspicious.
The mighty archers, afraid of fighting at night, O Bharata, then withdrew together with all their horses.
When the Kauravas had gone, O king, at the end of the day, the Parthas, glad at heart, having won, went to their own camp.
With sounds of many instruments, lion-roars and dancing, mocking their foes and praising Achyuta and Arjuna,
when the retreat was sounded by those heroes, all the soldiers, O lords of men, bestowed blessings upon the Pandavas.
Then, the retreat done, the Kurus and Pandavas, delighted, went to their camps at night and the kings entered them.
Yakshas, rakshasas, pishachas and beasts of prey in hosts went to the dreadful battlefield, like the dancing ground of Rudra.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Partha alone carried off Bhadra, alone satisfied Agni, and alone, having conquered this earth, made kings pay tribute.
Alone with his divine bow he slew the Nivatakavachas, and alone fought Sharva, standing in the form of a Kirata.
Alone he protected the Bharatas, alone he pleased Bhava. By that one man all my fierce-spirited men were conquered; they are not to be blamed but praised. Tell me what they did."
[Sanjaya said:] Struck, beaten, shattered, without armour, weapons or mounts, with dejected voices, tormented, proud ones conquered by their foes,
the Kauravas in their camp again took counsel, like serpents with broken fangs, poison gone, trodden underfoot.
Then Karna, enraged, sighing like a serpent, pressing hand with hand, looking at your son, said to them:

Arjuna is always alert, firm, skilled and steadfast, and Adhokshaja (Krishna) instructs him in the right time.
mahabharata:8:22.9	By his release of a thousand weapons we have today been cheated; but tomorrow I will, O lord of the earth, destroy all his designs.
Thus addressed, saying "So be it," he dismissed the best of kings; having rested happily through the night, glad, they went out to battle.
They saw the formation arranged by the king of dharma, hard to conquer, carefully made by the chief of the Kurus after the doctrines of Brihaspati and Ushanas.
Then Duryodhana remembered Karna, bull-shouldered, ever the opponent of the self-conquered.
His mind went to Karna, the charioteer's son, mighty archer, equal to Purandara in battle, to the Maruts in strength and to Kartavirya in valour, like a friend in times of danger.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "When your minds, fools, went to Karna, Vaikartana, then did you see him, like the cold-tormented see the sun?
When the troops had been withdrawn and the battle began again, how did Vaikartana Karna fight there, Sanjaya, and how did all the Pandavas fight the charioteer's son?

Karna alone, the mighty-armed, could kill the Parthas with the Somakas; the might of Karna's arms is deemed equal to Shakra's and Vishnu's, so also his dreadful weapons and the valour of the great soul.
Seeing Duryodhana then severely tormented by the Pandava, and seeing the sons of Pandu valiant in the great battle,
Duryodhana, relying on Karna in the battle, again takes pride, and Karna is eager to conquer the Parthas with their sons and with Keshava.
Ah, great sorrow, that violent Karna did not defeat the sons of Pandu in the battle! Fate is surely the refuge. Ah, this dreadful end of the dice game is now upon us!
Ah, the sharp sorrows made by Duryodhana, I shall bear them, Sanjaya, dreadful, like thorns.
And Subala's son too, dear one, thinks himself prudent.
While these divine battles were going on, Sanjaya, I heard constantly that my sons were slain and beaten.
There is none to hold back the Pandavas in battle; they plunge in like into a company of women; fate is indeed stronger."
[Sanjaya said:] "One who thinks afterwards of a duty already past, that duty is not done for him, and he is destroyed by brooding.
But this duty of yours, knowing it to have gone far, you did not do before, in considering what was gained and not gained.
You were told in many ways, O king, by the Pandavas, 'Do not fight'; you did not accept it out of delusion, O lord of men, toward the Pandavas.
You have done terrible wrongs to the sons of Pandu; for you this dreadful destruction of kings is going on.
Therefore, having passed that, do not grieve, O best of the Bharatas; hear everything as it happened, the dreadful slaughter, O unfallen one.
When the night had turned to dawn, Karna came to the king, and the mighty-armed one, meeting Duryodhana, said:
'Today, O king, I shall meet the glorious Pandava; I shall slay that hero, or he will slay me.
Because of the multitude of my tasks and of Partha's, O king, there has been no meeting between me and Arjuna.
But hear this word of mine according to my understanding, O lord of men: I shall not return, O Bharata, without having slain Partha in battle.
When this army's heroes are slain and I stand in battle, Partha will attack me, bereft of Shakra's dart.
Then understand what is for your good, O lord of men, concerning the power of weapons and the equipment of Arjuna.
In piercing a great body, in lightness, in long-range shooting, in skill and in application of weapons, Savyasachin is not my equal.
The bow named Vijaya, the great minister of all weapons, was made by Vishvakarma for Indra, who desired it.
With it Shatakratu conquered hosts of daityas, O king; at its sound the ten quarters of the daityas grew confused. Shakra gave that supremely esteemed bow to Bhargava.
Bhargava gave that excellent divine bow to me, with which I shall fight the mighty-armed Arjuna, best of victors, as Indra in battle fought all the assembled daityas.
That dreadful bow given by Rama surpasses Gandiva; with that bow the earth was conquered three times seven times.
The divine feats of that bow Bhargava told of; Rama gave it to me, with which I shall fight the Pandava.
Today, Duryodhana, I shall delight you with your kinsmen by slaying in battle the hero Arjuna, best of victors.
Today, O king, the earth with her mountains, forests, islands and seas, with her foes slain, will be established for your sons and grandsons.
Nothing is impossible for me today, especially for your sake; for one rightly devoted to dharma, success comes like that of the self-controlled.
He cannot withstand me in battle as a tree cannot withstand fire. But I must say in what respect I am inferior to Phalguna.
His bowstring is divine, and his two great quivers inexhaustible; his excellent divine bow Gandiva is ageless in battle.
And Vijaya is a great divine excellent bow of mine too; in that, O king, I am superior to Partha with that bow.
But the Pandava hero is superior to me in this—learn it from me: his charioteer is the Dasharha (Krishna), honoured by all the world.
His divine chariot, gift of Agni, adorned with gold, is unbreakable on every side, O hero; his horses are swift as thought, and his divine, radiant banner bearing a monkey causes wonder.
Krishna, creator of the world, guards that chariot. Lacking these things, I wish to fight the Pandava.
But this hero Shalya, ornament of assemblies, equal to him—if he would be my charioteer, your victory would be sure.
Let Shalya be my charioteer, to the discomfort of the enemy; let carts carry iron arrows and vulture-feathered arrows for me.
And let the chief chariots, O king of kings, yoked with the best horses, always follow behind me, O best of the Bharatas.
Thus I shall be superior to Partha in qualities. Shalya is superior to Krishna, and I am superior to Arjuna.
As the Dasharha, slayer of heroes, knows the heart of horses, so Shalya too, the great chariot-warrior, knows horses.
In the strength of arms none is equal to the king of the Madras, and none among bowmen is my equal in weapons.
And in the driving of horses none is equal to Shalya; so my chariot will be superior to Partha's.
This, O great king, I desire to be done by you, scorcher of foes; when this is done, all my desires will be fulfilled.
Then you will see in battle what I shall do, O Bharata; in every way I shall conquer today all the assembled Pandavas.'
[Duryodhana said:] 'I shall do all this as you think fit, Karna; chariots with their equipment and horses will follow you, charioteer's son.
Let carts carry iron arrows and vulture-feathered arrows for you; we and all the kings shall follow you, Karna.'"
[Sanjaya said:] Having said this, O great king, your valiant son went up to the king of the Madras and spoke these words.

O truthful, illustrious one, increaser of the sins of your foes, lord of the Madras, hero in battle, terror of enemy armies,
mahabharata:8:23.3	you have heard Karna speak, O best of speakers; in the midst of the lion-like kings he chooses you.
mahabharata:8:23.4	Therefore, for Partha's destruction and for my good, O best of charioteers, you should willingly become his charioteer.
mahabharata:8:23.5	In the world there is no other rein-holder equal to you; protect Karna on every side as Brahma protects Shankara.
mahabharata:8:23.6	As Krishna, the excellent rein-holder, is Partha's counsellor, so you too protect Radheya on every side.
mahabharata:8:23.7	Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, you, the valiant Bhoja, Subala's son Shakuni, Drona's son and I are our strength; the army, O lord of the host, has been divided into nine parts among them.
mahabharata:8:23.8	In this there was no share of Bhishma and the great-souled Drona; having surpassed those two shares, my enemies have been slain.
mahabharata:8:23.9	Those two aged tigers among men were slain by deceit, having done a deed not easy to do, and gone to heaven from here, sinless one.
mahabharata:8:23.12	As Krishna is the excellent rein-holder of Partha in battle, yoked with him, Partha is protected in battle, O king, and the deeds he does are visible, just so are yours.
mahabharata:8:23.13	Before, Arjuna did not slay his enemies in battle thus; day after day, lord of the Madras, he is seen routing them in the fight.
mahabharata:8:23.14	The share of Karna and yours remains, O greatly splendid one; destroy that share together with Karna at once in battle.
mahabharata:8:23.15	As darkness vanishes on seeing the sun and its dawn, O revered one, so let the sons of Kunti with the Panchalas and Srinjayas perish.
mahabharata:8:23.16	Karna is the foremost of chariot-warriors and you are the foremost of charioteers; in the world there is none to match the pair of you in encounter.
mahabharata:8:23.17	As the Varshneya (Krishna) protects the Pandava in all circumstances, so protect Karna, son of Vikartana, in battle.
mahabharata:8:23.18	With you as charioteer he will be unassailable even by the gods with Shakra in battle, O lord of the earth; how much less by the Pandavas—do not doubt my word.
Hearing Duryodhana's words, Shalya, filled with anger, making a three-lined frown and shaking his hands again and again,
Having duly made Shalya his commander, the king, best of kings, went out to battle with the surviving kings.
My son, young, of thunderbolt body, not to be slain by any being, was killed in battle by the Pandavas, Sanjaya.
In due order perform the funeral rites for fathers, sons and grandsons, kinsmen, friends and elders.
On the holy bank of Bhagirathi, hundreds of thousands of Brahmanas consoled the king, whose mind was distraught with grief.
[Bhishma said:] "Why do you regard yourself as dependent and as the cause? This matter of action is subtle and beyond the senses, O great one."
Enjoy it with your brothers and friends, O lord of men; I see nothing for you to grieve over, best of upholders of dharma.
Kunti, daughter of Kuntibhoja, followed Gandhari, as did Draupadi, Subhadra and the other Pandava women, who behaved alike toward those two, the parents-in-law, as was fitting.
[Vaishampayana said:] Then in the thirty-sixth year a great calamity befell the Vrishnis; urged by Time, they slew one another with pestles.
This son of your son will be the Kuru king, and Vajra has been made king, the remnant of the Yadavas.
For whose sake the whole earth, friends and kinsmen were slain by us violently in battle, afflicted earlier in the great forest—
